title: Master Ma is Unwell
speaker: Reizan Bob Penny
summary: Reizan Bob Penny's dharma talk emphasizes the importance of embracing grief and sadness as a natural part of life, rather than trying to avoid or escape them. By confronting our own history of grief and accepting both the pain and the beauty that come with it, we can find intimacy and healing through shared concern and connection with others. This acceptance is not about avoiding difficult emotions, but about surrendering to them in a way that allows us to heal and transform.
topics: Zen story about Master Mao Tzu

sentences.text: Good afternoon.
As I get into this talk, I wanted to start by saying a few things about the practice period we've been experiencing together for the last number of weeks.
It's been a really wonderful experience for me, and I've felt honored to serve everyone here in this role.
I've got to know many of you in new ways that I didn't know before, and I hope to continue that as we go forward.
I know this practice period has touched a lot of people in various ways, and I hope it's been fruitful and meaningful for all of you.
We go into these sorts of things somewhat blind, not knowing what to expect.
I think if we knew what was coming, we wouldn't do something like this in the first place.
To do it at all, we have to go in blind just to get ourselves in the door.
In regard to being shuso, that's certainly been true for me.
But also, no one signs up to be personally challenged in ways they might not feel capable of handling.
And no one comes into life welcoming loss and personal tragedy.
There's been plenty of that over the last few months within our Sangha.
Our topic for the classes I've been facilitating this last month has been practicing with grief.
I really had no idea how personal this would be for many in our group when I first decided on the class topic back in September or early October.
I was actually feeling, believe it or not, that at least in terms of myself, I was choosing a safe subject.
It was something I figured I knew something about from personal experience and could therefore probably say a few things about.
But it was also mostly in my past, and therefore not so charged for me that I couldn't take it up.
In other words, I tricked myself into it.
In exploring grief, I discovered that I really hadn't gotten around all the losses I've had in my life as I thought I had.
There were many people from my life to think about and hold in memorial in a way I hadn't really done yet.
And there has been, I found, a lot more for me to learn about my own process, which has tended, I discovered, toward the ungrounded side of things.
A sort of wandering soul orphan persona I've had going on, not yet settled from the ruptures of my past.
But it was just following my deciding on the class topic that Sangha members here began experiencing a series of close family losses.

A couple of days ago I checked in with Tim, who's been facilitating the memorial services for most all of these people, to see if I could get straight in my mind how many people have recently passed away since October.
We came up with nine.
These have been a mother, a sister, a niece, an uncle, a son, two mother-in-laws, a close family friend, and one Sangha member who had been sitting with us here in this zendo.
Close family relations.
Two of these losses happened to people attending the grief class, and they each had to miss one of the classes on grief to go off and have real passages of grief in their own lives.
My own ex-mother-in-law passed away during the practice period.
It's been encouraging to me that people from the class have told me that things from the class have had a direct impact on their current processes with loss.
In the classes we've discussed how each of us has our own history of grief that we bring to each new loss, a history we may not be completely aware of.
We've spent time exploring the felt sensations of grief: the heat, the coldness of it, the weight and gravity it has.
We've experimented with new labels to describe the complex of feelings we each have about it.
We've studied grieving styles and explored how we each might benefit from learning about a different style than the one we habitually found ourselves within.
And we've looked at the pervasive, more global aspects of grief: how societies relate to loss, a threat of loss and a threatened planet, and how our own personal grief is set within that context.
But it seems that with what has been going on in our Sangha, this subject is following us at least as closely, if not more closely, than we are following it.
So although I could perhaps speak today about a variety of things, I'm going to talk again about grief.
What I'll talk about is the issue we've danced around throughout the class but not yet settled into, which is acceptance.
To help focus on this, I'm going to talk about a case from the Book of Serenity.
Norman suggested that I look at this, and I hope I do some justice to it.
It's also mentioned in the Blue Cliff Record, and it involves the same person that Norman discussed in his talk this morning, Master Ma Tzu.
The case is "Master Ma Is Unwell."
It's generally assumed in this story that Master Ma is very ill, perhaps gravely ill, and has been bedridden for some time.
The case in Cleary's translation goes:
*Master Ma was unwell.
The monastery superintendent asked, "Master, how is your venerable state these days?"
The great teacher said, "Sun-faced Buddha, moon-faced Buddha."*
These Zen stories are given to us in a distilled format that requires a little explanation, especially since we don't have the right kind of context to put them in.
The reference to sun-faced Buddha and moon-faced Buddha is from the Butsu Myoho, a text listing 11,093 names of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
In it, the sun-faced Buddha is described as living for 1,800 years, and the moon-faced Buddha lives for one day and one night.
There seems to be a poetic logic in these names, because the sun is always, to our senses, the same, round and full.
It does not wax and wane like the moon, which, to close observation, is visibly seen to change each day, to literally be a different moon.
And yet Master Ma has set these both together, equally, as if to say, long life or short life, but all still Buddha.
Perhaps there are other meanings.
In the same way that these stories obscure their meaning, in a way, they also allow meaning to unfold in multiple ways.
It's always important to consider the other characters in these stories, I think, and not just the teacher who dispenses the punchline, so to speak.
These stories all come from real life, lives just like our own lives of gain and loss.
The monastery superintendent asks, "Master, how is your venerable state these days?"
In the Blue Cliff Record, this character is called the Chief Accountant, and he asks, "Sir, during these recent days, how is your health?"
Here I'll take my own path and take issue with some commentary that I found in the Book of Serenity, and take an opposite point of view.
The commentator says, everyday matters keep him so busy, he seldom gets to inquire about someone's health.
He's made out to be some sort of busy pencil pusher, and Master Ma is made out to be the one who shakes him up.
But I think this is an unfair picture of the superintendent.
I see the superintendent in contrast to the young man we heard about previously this weekend.
This is no novice, no newbie who traveled far only to call the great teacher a log bridge.
When you think about a log bridge, it's not even hardly a bridge.
It's like the first evolution of bridge beyond stone hopping.
It's usually a found thing, like, there's a log, let's cross here.
So, a pretty cutting remark.
But certainly Master Ma's monastery was a large affair.
The superintendent or chief accountant would have been someone of seniority whom Master Ma knew well.
And Master Ma is not simply someone.
Certainly if the great teacher was gravely bedridden, this would be utmost in the minds of the monastery staff.
When I was 15 years old, I was in the hospital for a week.
They thought I had appendicitis, but after taking out the appendix they decided it really was intestinal flu.
To make it worse, I didn't find that out for three days.
So the operation of course hadn't really helped the flu at all.
Instead I had the flu and a big incision in my abdomen.
I was pretty miserable, and having intestinal flu is not very pretty.
Each day my mother would come in and she would ask, "Have you had any more episodes?"
Well, I'd been having episodes pretty regularly, like clockwork, about every two hours for days.
But in between times I was doing fairly okay.
You could call it sun-faced Buddha, moon-faced Buddha, I suppose.
But I never came up with anything so pithy and poetic as Master Ma.
Instead I would usually say a bit too much more than she wanted to hear.
There was little she could do for me, and I took her daily inquiry as concern.
In fact, I welcomed it.
It was the limit to which her mothering could be exercised in the situation: to keep an inquiry going with me, to monitor my condition, even if there was nothing she could do.
I think something like this is going on in this exchange.
Perhaps Master Ma's condition, like mine had been, had its ups and downs.
The superintendent is asking with some decorum and out of obvious concern if it's been a good day or a bad day in the general course of Master Ma's decline.
And the teacher answers as if to say, some days I feel I will live forever and some days I feel it's my last day.
But he combines this with saying, and all things are Buddha.
I think we would be really missing the point if we assumed that the trick of these Zen stories is to figure out just how clever and brilliant the teacher is being in the situation.

That view has been given to us, maybe, in the popularization of Zen a number of decades ago: an idea that these crafty and wise Zen masters always had the advantage and could turn the minds of their students with a few well-placed and cutting remarks.
As if the intimacy that passes all understanding could best be achieved through a put-down.
Instead, it's the intimacy of shared concern that I think is evident here.
Master Ma is saying all things are Buddha, even death is Buddha.
Buddha is nowhere if not in sickness, old age and death.
In this way Master Ma is compassionately assisting the superintendent's process of grief.
Suzuki Roshi has said, "We die and we do not die.
That is the right understanding."
Similarly, Master Ma is saying that to live one day or for endless lifetimes is all still Buddha.
Acceptance in the grieving process comes only in these small moments, really.
A word or two, a felt presence, and something shifts.
Some resolution is gained, sadness plays itself out, and afterwards grief is seen as a new level of intimacy, as something gained, perhaps, rather than lost.
A gain in appreciation, in love, and in gratitude.
Zen stories are usually about some moment when a shift happens.
An opening is passed and through it the world has changed a bit.

I think this brief exchange between Master Ma and the monastery superintendent is such a moment, in which the superintendent gains acceptance for the grief he's feeling over the great teacher's illness and eventual passing.
It's a story of one of those times when a few healing words have the opportunity to be spoken while a person is still alive.
A few words which resolve many things.
Suzuki Roshi commented on this case and said:
*Once you realize Buddha nature within and without, there is no special way to follow for a student or any specific suggestion to give for a teacher.
When there is a problem, there is the way to go.
Actually, you continuously go over and over the great path of the Buddha with your teacher who is always with you.*
The problem in this story that Suzuki Roshi mentions is grief.
Here he says that being connected, traveling the path, these things never cease.
When intimacy is reached, there is nothing specific that a teacher and a student, a mother and a son, or any two people with an intimate connection need to do.
Now, some of you know that I've made it a practice for many years to work closely at times with the I Ching.
For periods of time I've been very consistent with this.
My practice has been to consult the oracle open-endedly, without a specific question, each evening.
Years ago I would take this a little further and write down a small phrase that stood out from the reading on a little slip of paper.
I would put this in my pocket, and during the next day I would pull it out from time to time and puzzle for a moment on it.
One day about six or seven years after my father died, I had a very strange experience of resolution in connection with this practice.
I actually haven't ever told too many people about it, because it just seemed a bit of an unusual experience.
But I came to realize that on this day the I Ching had been directing me towards an opening for acceptance of my grief.

The hexagram that came up was called Work on What Has Been Spoiled, and it seemed on the surface to relate to some sort of past transgression of either my mother or my father that I needed to resolve.
Now I see that this work, the problem, as Suzuki Roshi mentions, was working on resolving grief.
This was especially so in the case of the one specific line that I drew, which read:
*Setting right what has been spoiled by the father, if there is a son, no blame.
Rest upon the departed father, danger in the end good fortune.*
And then there was this addendum:
*Setting right what has been spoiled by the father, he receives in his thoughts the deceased father.*
I could understand from all of this that I was to resolve my grief over my father's passing, to set right what was spoiled.
I could see that as the son, some responsibility rested with me to do this grief work, and that my father's death need not be a continued source of pain, hence no blame.
I could see the difficulty, danger, and a sense that in the end there could be good fortune.
I've currently been exploring all of this in therapy fairly intensely, so I could see all these connections.
But what was this line, "he receives in his thoughts the deceased father"?
I had no idea what this meant, but I copied it down and put it in my pocket for the next day.
The next day I had to drop off my partner somewhere for a while and I ended up having a couple of hours to kill, so I went for a walk in the snowy woods.
I was living in Vermont.
As usual with my I Ching consultations, I purposely kept doing a partial focus on the reading from the night before during my days.
I had forgotten what it was that the slip of paper in my pocket said.
It hadn't occurred to me yet to even look at it that day.
As I was walking, no particular place to go, I came to a log and sat down for a short while.
It was then that this very strange thing happened.
It was a daydream, in the literal sense of the word.
Not some distracted imagination, but a lucid vision where, in a very quiet and alone moment, reality slipped a little bit and it was as though I was dreaming while I was still awake.
It all happened in the space of about three seconds.
I perceived my father sitting beside me on the log in the same posture I was, a ghostly apparition of sorts.
Then his body simply floated sideways and merged into my body and disappeared.
At that moment I felt something, very subtle, but a shift.
Ever since then I've never had the same sort of sadness about his death as I had before.
It was only later that I thought to check what phrase I'd gathered from the I Ching the night before for that day.
I hope that for those of you here who have recently lost someone in your lives, some version of your own of that kind of experience might happen someday for you.
Acceptance is not a washing away of all grief or an end to the grieving process.
Acceptance is simply another step.
Then there is grief beyond acceptance.
Grief is a process unfolding in time, and therefore new occasions for grief concerning a loss continue onward throughout life.
The question is, has your grief found healing in acceptance?
Has the pain and sadness of your loss found a new level where grief is now not so much a sadness about what is gone but is instead a poignant gratitude for what was given?
Sun-faced Buddha, moon-faced Buddha.
Sun-faced Buddha lives almost forever in this sense.
No one ever dies.
We can never lose anyone or be separated from anyone.
Moon-faced Buddha lives only one day and one night.
In this way we are each unique, never to be seen again.
Even the you that you are right now today will never be seen again.
The introduction to this case from the Book of Serenity goes:
*Even investigating beyond mind, intellect and consciousness, there is still this.
Even studying in ordinary and holy paths, it's already too exalted.
The red-hot furnace spurts out iron barbs.
With tongue-sword and lip-spear, it's hard to open the mouth without running afoul of the point.
Please try to bring it up.*
Grief is deep and pervasive.
It's an emotion, an emotional process and an almost palpable bodily wound that requires healing.
To run from it is to never be free from it.
Yet exploring it goes through mind, intellect and consciousness.
At the end of grief is still this: Buddha, beyond life, not separate from life.
Although it's certainly difficult, although it seems that each time we try, we run afoul of our own process, we still have to try.
And so it says, "Please try to bring it up."
That right there is the best advice, I think.
If you don't know what to do, if your sadness feels overwhelming, if you have no idea how you will go forward, just try to bring it up.
Find one person.
One person who will take the time to listen, to whatever you have to say.
Even if you feel you are running afoul of the point and not getting anywhere, not making sense, it doesn't matter.
The healing happens through intimacy and through small changes, which are beyond what you think you can figure out, even beyond anything you imagine might help.
You have to surrender to grief and accept that grief is now a part of life, a place where you need to touch intimacy to heal.
Well, the practice period is almost over.
I just want to say thank you again for the opportunity to be your Shuso for this period of time.
It's been very transformative for me.
And I just look forward to all the years in the future practicing together.
Thanks.
